reviews.text: > Pulled teeth from a guy until his power changed to 'strength equal to the number of teeth pulled this game'. > My toothless army became unstoppable. > Fed so many pies to a hippo the game lagged whenever I drew him > Fed more pies. > Got shot. Turned getting shot into money. Turned getting shot into long term power. > died anyway. A clever and quirky deckbuilder that breaks the mould of a saturated genre. There's a little bit of balatro, a little bit of slay the spire, a lot all it's own. There's tons of weird interactions and obscure combos, if you like theory crafting how to make a specific card good, you're gonna have a good time. I playtested this game and must apologise for helping find some of the most broken combos--but there are lots more to discover.

The combat mechanics themselves are interesting, but the balance in this game is awful and full of "gotcha" mechanics. I played two runs before I decided to refund it, so I'll give you my experience: FIRST RUN Still learning the game, but it's not too bad. I notice that the wheel spin location is way too swingy against the player to ever be worth it (Would you like a 50/50 chance to either make 10 gold or permanently lose one of your fighters???), and that my current map seed is full of them. Okay, fine, whatever. Some of the other locations, like the Dentist, are actually interesting, so it isn't all bad. I make it past the first two chapters of the act with relative ease, only to come across a location in the third chapter called "Foreign Envoy". This is one of those "gotcha" moments I was talking about. It asks if you want to make all of your soldiers educated with a bunch of other buffs. It turns out that 'educated' makes all of your fighters have negative values now. Meaning that you are basically screwed with no way to roll it back. There's an achievement for it, so it's obvious that the developers just want to be cheeky, but I'm not a fan of having 40 minutes of my life wasted because of a random event. SECOND RUN Fine. First round ended because the devs wanted to troll me. Next run, I come to a location called Horse Betting. You can take a free ticket if you think the horse will make it all the way, or pay money to gamble on it making it only as far as the first or second checkpoint. It says there's a 96% chance of making it to the first checkpoint, so for five gold, I pay. The horse immediately collapses over and I get nothing. Bad luck or more dev trolling? At this point, I have no idea, but I'm not here for it. Annoyed, but I like the base combat well enough, so I continue. I make it pretty far, even as the boards randomly (and permanently) kill some of my strongest units. I'm at the boss of chapter four though, so I figure if I make good decisions, maybe I can still pull out a win. The boss's mechanic is that they erase the modifiers you've paid for in each column and replace them with something else. So if, like me, you spent most of your gold on x2, x3, x4, x5 multipliers, you now get the pleasure of watching them turn into -1, -2, -6, etc. If I'm playing Slay the Spire and the boss just literally tells me to play with a different deck, then what's the point? Is this just another gotcha moment where you don't invest in the board because the boss is going to ♥♥♥♥ it no matter what? CONCLUSION I've experienced enough of the game (luckily within the refund window) to know that this isn't for me. I'm sure there'll be people that say the whole point of a roguelike is for the dev to waste as much of your time as possible (git gud at RNG bro!), but I disagree. The above experiences should give you enough of a clue whether you'll agree or disagree too.

Gonna leave a positive review, because I feel like it's another Wildfrost situation: cute and great graphics, innovative and fun gameplay, lots of cool game mechanics, but extremely, deceivingly punishing gameplay loop that's so hard to grasp it feels unfair. So leaving a negative review feels unfair - at least since I haven't devoted enough hours to this game yet. That being said, The Royal Writ is extremely hard to get into. The tooltips' wording isn't all that clear and at times I struggle to understand why I'm losing cards during the battle. The Balatro-style modifier seems to miss the point that in Balatro each card has a blue value that you can multiply by a red one. The Royal Writ cards don't necessarily have a blue value and it creates frustration when you draw all-red cards that ultimately amount to zero. Even giving them a value of 1 would amount to something. The bosses in this game are extra hard to beat. I feel like you need to actively look and plan ahead for a boss fight, since its mechanics might flip your winning strategy on its head. It's clever, but also feels overwhelming at times. I'm not entirely sure how to consistently win against them yet. Other than challenging gameplay and perhaps some balancing issues, the Royal Writ feels a lot of fun to play and the way it handles the secret card abilities is simply perfect. It's a very clever game, I hope it'll get polished to perfection soon

This is a pretty fun and silly game until Act 2, when basically every element of the gameplay loop is...acting against you. Not in a tradeoff as you might expect, where a strong effect is balanced against a strong risk; nor is it simply an increased difficulty, like "ascension" runs in many deckbuilders. Most of the cards and mechanics in Act 2 are simply exhausting to play with. The cards are mostly bad; they kill themselves or drain your Morale or inflict status on themselves for negligible effects; many of them perpetually fill your hand with junk cards that aren't very useful most of the time and prevent you from drawing into useful cards. Out of the pool of cards I've unlocked in Act 2 (maybe 12 or so) I actively avoid most of them; there are 3 I want. Some of them I'm not even sure how you're supposed to use them, or why you would want to. It's possible there are strategies I'm missing, but it seems more likely that this is an intentional thematic design that fits the "story" of the second act.

游戏的画风和音乐很棒，很用心，值得一试。但是游戏本身的设计有自限性问题，很难让人沉浸其中并获得爽感。 具体而言，首先，游戏里的负面效果远比正面效果要多得多，这就导致几乎玩家的每个选择都在努力规避负面效果，而不是专注于放大正面效果，获得快速正反馈。甚至于，游戏里每一个可能带来爽感的遗物或者卡牌，都有绑定的负面效果，需要小心地去规避。甚至为了解决一个负面效果，你好不容易拿到的解法，自身又带来了另一个负面效果。这会让人很累，而且即便千辛万苦最终成型，也只是会长舒口气，而不是获得强大的成就感。 其次，游戏把玩家的卡牌限制的很死，鼓励“养大哥”式build，每种厉害的build最终就两三张“大哥”。这就导致过程中的很多选择、很多牌，都是流水式地过牌走流程，尤其很多“大哥”都是“走一步加一攻击”这种纯被动养成。这会导致游戏的很多体验变成对耐心的考研，让玩家陷入“怎么还抽不到”，“怎么又是这种”，“怎么又debuff了”的烦躁循环里。同时，还得花很大精力去把废牌处理掉，从而不超上限。另一方面，因为只有两三张大哥，所以形成多张牌的联动combo的爽感几乎是很难实现的，反而因为各种失误一旦“大哥”废了，就会满盘皆输。总之，这样的设计会大大限制游戏本身的深度和多样性，鼓励简单粗暴的过关方式，而不是一个个优秀的选择的优势积累。 最后，还想吐槽下游戏里的引导系统，以及文本解释和翻译，对于新手非常不友好。很多机制也没有好好解释和引导，让人很难理解机制的运作，进而打错、乌龙却不自知(比如中毒后吃馅饼不加基础攻击；比如行军机制不算分可以多刷被动）。 总之，我觉得游戏的底子很好，但机制上有很多大改的空间，希望制作组能又后续的update。

This is a very difficult game to evaluate for me, and is absolutely one of those titles where I wish Steam allowed for a more nuanced review system than "I recommend" or "I do not recommend." There are a lot of things here to like. The artstyle, for one, slaps, and is absolutely the best strength of the game. The music is very good, and there's a neat little story to accompany/contextualise your runs. It's not groundbreaking, but it also doesn't need to be. The story is neither obtrusive nor boring, so it's a neat little flavouring. Unfortunately, there are enough rough edges to make the experience wonky. The tutorial doesn't do a great job of teaching you the game's mechanics beyond the bare minimum, and the in-game journal that describes the rules is only two pages long and omits a lot. There's also some ludonarrative dissonance. Narratively, the game makes no justification for why your cards improve in strength as they advance towards the enemy, or why cards *have* to advance even if doing so would kill themselves. This doesn't ruin the game, of course, but it makes for a weird texture - it's hard to describe. The name of each card is capitalised but their epithets aren't. Similarly, there's a few sentences in-game that should have punctuation, but don't. This obviously isn't a show-stopper or anything, but indicates a lack of polish and care. The calculator to show you how much damage you're currently doing has an animation, for some reason, so you have to wait to see the final number. Why? It's not like the animation is concealing some background computation that takes time to do - it's multiplying two numbers. There are some cards with a random effect when you play them. Some of these cards have the odds listed out, while some don't. Why? I'm assuming that if the odds aren't listed, it's an even chance of each effect happening, but I shouldn't have to make that assumption. Just write the odds on the card. A lot of cards have weird phrasing on their abilities that make them difficult to parse what they actually do, how they interact with other cards/mechanics, etc. It feels a lot like how early Yu-gi-oh cards read, before problem-solving card text. This is a pretty large sin to me. I want to know exactly what a card does before I play it for the first time; I don't want to have to experiment with how something works and potentially lose a run because I guessed an interaction wrong. The game could do with a lot of rules-writing streamlining to make cards and abilities read more intuitively, using the same language as one another. As an example, in my first run, I ran across a card with an ability that triggered when I fed it something, but I hadn't encountered food cards yet, and neither the tutorial nor the in-game rules booklet tell you what food is and how you feed it to cards. Queue me scratching my head for the rest of the run on how to actually use this card's ability. That kind of confusion could be easily avoided if "being fed" was bolded or italicised to inform you that it means something specific, and if food cards had a tag or category or something to explicitly tell you that yes, this is food. Also, it should be in the rules book. That goes without saying. Ultimately, it's hard to recommend this one. Maybe on sale, maybe if you're *really* into rogue-lite deckbuilders, but there is no shortage of those these days.

Edit: After beating the first Act, and playing some more it becomes more fun as you better understand the mechanics. Most people won't do the tutorial, me included. So your job is to either highlight that the tutorial is short and provide a number of minutes needed to accomplish it, or better yet provide glossary on screen that clearly explains the effect of poison, frail, and the different food types. It may be that you intend it to be an old school rogue-like where you had to figure out the effects on your own, but the art style does not give that impression. So it is misleading, at least for me. Weird game, there is no progression as such. The story is meh. The gameplay so far is pretty barebones, and the onboarding and glossary is a terrible experience. The only thing I can appreciate is the music and the aesthetics. Not enough.

全通关来评价： 最近，《小丑牌》的卡牌构筑机制在独立游戏设计中很受欢迎，其核心在于分数相乘的算分方式与肉鸽玩法的叠加。很多游戏试图在此框架下探索更多样化的可能性，此游戏便是其一。 此游戏在延续该框架的基础上，引入了排兵布阵、子弹射击等全新战斗机之，并结合了类似《杀戮尖塔》的地图推进系统。在战斗中，玩家需要布下士兵，达到分数以击败敌人，而战斗间有各式各样的事件可以构筑牌堆。游戏分一、二两幕，两幕的卡牌完全不同，可以当作两个游戏分别对待。整体而言，第一幕较为简单，而第二幕更难（难度与《小丑牌》相当？） 从我的角度来看，我愿意给好评。游戏画风可爱，配乐和谐，整体氛围轻松。排兵布阵的机制很上头，大部分的游玩时间都是在战斗内考虑应该怎么布阵。但是游戏机制上也有一些缺点： 首先，内容深度不足。游戏整体思路就是找成长牌，养数值。卡牌之间有一些有意思的配合，但数量有限。尤其是第二幕，由于最终boss机制和前面一路上遇到的都有较大差别，只有依赖少数几种套路才能通关，所以很多能一路顺利通关的牌组会折在最后，就很恼火。 其次，游戏debuff太重，还不好解。比如第一幕玩馅饼，如果吃中毒了，没找到解法后续馅饼直接废了。第二幕debuff满天飞，看似不得不拥抱并利用debuff了，但实际上只有出血可以利用，其它debuff还是用不了。那些描述中负累会变化的卡根本没法用。 与前两点都相关的，游戏高度依赖sl。游戏中有大量随机性，比如食物吃完到底是给buff还是debuff，子弹出现位置、种类等等。像之前说的，很多情况下被上了debuff或者排得不巧导致士兵死了会直接导致崩盘，所以非常依赖sl（以及刷开局找成长牌）。 最后，第二幕的最终boss需要单独吐槽一下。本身间谍牌数值就不强：多数情况金币士气要么都缺要么都不缺，来回转没啥用；给食物的纯纯负收益（给debuff/占牌堆），完了你最后boss再给上那么一个debuff谁还玩间谍牌？还有那个议员，反正我每次都是固定先把他找出来然后重开的，把他藏起来纯属恶心人，毫无意义。 此外我还有一些小的评论： 1 中文翻译太烂。不是生硬，而是不准，有很强的误导性。比如“can blow on the wonderwheel more than once”翻译成“可以多次转动奇迹圆盘”，这意思完全变了。 2 关键词索引不全。索引是好文明，可惜不全，比如“触发一张子弹”是什么意思？ 3 希望可以在卡上标明卡牌的稀有度。 4 第二幕不管在打难度几最后通关后都显示“难度10已解锁”。 总体而言游戏是值得推荐的。虽然在价格对标《小丑牌》的情况下可能不及《小丑牌》的高度，但还是推荐喜欢《小丑牌》的玩家一试。
美术、音乐都很好，但不好玩，无聊，单调，负反馈又多，让人觉得自己既不幸运又不聪明，玩了不少的卡牌肉鸽游戏，这款是数一数二的内容少还折磨人，好评是因为朋友送的，给友情好评不是给游戏好评。
那我问你制作人你自己玩过游戏么？作为一个卡牌肉鸽游戏，是这么做到卡牌设计如此弱智的，我的天这种游戏居然压根没有几个永久成长核心，那临时攻击力的体系一定很强吧，能不能把数值，卡牌触发条件这种基本理念搞清楚，还能整出一本道这种强制要求单体质量的关卡，纵排加攻的数值也高的离谱，配上强的离谱的陷阱和负面效果真有你的。

The Royal Writ is a roguelite deck builder card game, where you play the role of a king, who has set out at the countenance of his definitely-not-suspicious faceless berobed advisors, to quash those who would threaten your rule, including woodland bandits, an upstart octopus, a dancing goose, and among other things, your dad. You advance on a map from event to event slay the spire style, with a few battles in-between in each area, visiting shops, doing shady deals where you offer up a card and cash for something, spinning the 'wonderwheel', all in the pursuit of getting 'the good RNG' and having a strategy come together for your deck. Its quite fun, I found myself totally engrossed for hours in its charm. The gameplay is entertaining, if RNG dependent like most roguelite deckbuilders, but unlocking more content with each subsequent playthough helps keep things lively. Cards carry debuffs from battle to battle, which can sometimes be used to your advantage. The way you do damage in combat is somewhat reminiscent of Balatro, with cards split up into a flat damage, and others acting as mutipliers for that damage. Figuring out OP strategies is a large part of the fun, and in the second act I was immensely entertained by the synergy of promoting a bird midwife who generates child soldier 'spy' cards that do 5 damage each and debuff incoming bullets, which when used in turn, power up a 'dance master' goose to be more powerful, and then using an early retirement 'letter' card to return the midwife to my hand, play her again the next turn, and drop another stack of child soldiers to continue buffing the goose. I was very amused by this combo. The visual style for the game is great, the anthro characters are fun, I especially enjoyed the king haughtily strolling during the end scene after beating a boss with his royal retinue tromping in tow. The music is great, snappy and full of energy. You can kind of get a feel for the composers musical influences, which is quite likely Paper Mario: The Thousand Year Door (especially in the second act of the game.) You might pick up on some other samples in the music as well that seem awfully familiar (like Wario Land 4). The game is short, at just under 7 hours I've beaten both acts. There's still a fair bit of replayability with more cards to unlock, synergies to figure out, and a new 'hardship mode' that adds ways of making the game harder, but there isn't another act, which is kind of sad. The game is small but charming. I like pretty much everything about it except how it feels like there isn't enough of it, but that feeds into wanting to play it more. There is an 'endless mode', but when I tried playing it after beating the second act for the first time, it soft locked on me after the first battle, with all the events greyed-out, so I didn't bother. My verdict? Play the free demo, and see if it hooks you. I know it did for me.

I really wanted to recommend this game, but unfortunately the second Act significantly hurt the overall experience and enjoyment. TLDR: -The game suffers from a common roguelike/-lite issue: the more you unlock, the harder it becomes to reliably play specific & fun builds. -The balance feels overly random. If you don’t get the right cards, your run can fall apart through no fault of your own. -Many relics feel underwhelming or outright useless. -The death mechanic sounds interesting on paper, but in Act 2 it becomes frustrating, especially when combined with the bullet mechanic. -The bullet mechanic in Act 2 is often frustrating if you dont have a good build exploiting that mechanic. -Poison (especially in Act 2) can completely ruin a run if you don’t get the reliable cards to cleanse it. The first Act is genuinely great. While the randomness can still be a bit harsh for my taste, it’s much easier to put together fun and interesting builds. The new starting character I unlocked for Act 1 was also a blast to play and added a lot to the experience & variety. The second Act however, feels lackluster by comparison. I consistently struggled to get any kind of coherent/synergizing build going, and many runs felt doomed early due to bad RNG rather than poor decision-making. I’d really like to see the issues above addressed, or at least more cards options added (instead of 4 choices to pick from have 5 or 6 or make the rerolls way cheaper) especially in shops and events, so players have better tools to steer their builds instead of being at the mercy of randomness. Same with relics, just give us more to pick from when we have to choose. Based on the first Act alone, this would be a thumbs up. Unfortunately, the second Act counteracts that enjoyment, so my current verdict is a thumbs down. That said, I’m open to revisiting this if future updates improve the balance & randomness.

The Royal Writ, developed by Save Sloth Studios and published by Yogscast Games, is a roguelike deckbuilding game that sets itself apart by transforming cards into active participants on a battlefield rather than static actions. Instead of simply playing cards for immediate effects, each card represents a unit that physically advances across lanes toward an enemy objective. This design creates a blend of deckbuilding and positional strategy, where success depends not only on the strength of your deck but also on how you deploy and manage your units over time. The core gameplay revolves around carefully timing and placing units so they can advance across the battlefield and deal damage before being lost. Units grow in power as they move forward, creating a natural escalation that rewards patience and planning. However, once a unit reaches its target, it is removed from play, forcing players to constantly balance offense with sustainability. This system introduces a unique tension, as committing too many strong units early can leave you without resources later, while holding back may result in missed opportunities to deal critical damage. Deckbuilding is a central pillar of the experience, offering a wide variety of cards, relics, and modifiers that can significantly alter how each run unfolds. Players are encouraged to experiment with different combinations, building synergies that amplify their effectiveness. Some strategies may focus on maximizing damage output through stacking effects, while others emphasize control and careful positioning. The flexibility of the system allows for diverse playstyles, making each run feel distinct and encouraging repeated experimentation. As a roguelike, the game relies heavily on randomness to keep the experience fresh. Encounters, rewards, and events are procedurally generated, ensuring that no two playthroughs are exactly the same. This unpredictability adds excitement but also introduces an element of risk, as players must adapt to whatever options they are given. Over time, players unlock additional cards and upgrades, expanding their pool of possibilities and providing a sense of long-term progression that rewards persistence. The game’s structure is divided into multiple stages, each introducing new challenges and mechanics that build upon the core system. As players progress, they encounter increasingly complex scenarios that require a deeper understanding of timing and positioning. These additions help maintain engagement by preventing the gameplay from becoming repetitive, though they can also contribute to a steep learning curve. New mechanics are not always immediately intuitive, and players may need several attempts to fully grasp how to respond effectively. Visually, The Royal Writ adopts a colorful and stylized presentation that contrasts with its strategic depth. The characters and environments have a playful, almost storybook-like quality, which makes the game approachable at first glance. Beneath this lighthearted aesthetic, however, lies a system that demands careful thought and planning. The audio design complements this tone, with music and sound effects that enhance the atmosphere without overshadowing the gameplay. Despite its strengths, the game is not without its challenges. The reliance on random elements can sometimes lead to frustrating situations where success feels dependent on luck rather than skill. Certain encounters or combinations of events may be difficult to overcome regardless of preparation, which can make some runs feel unfair. Additionally, the complexity of the mechanics can be overwhelming for newcomers, as the game provides limited guidance and expects players to learn through trial and error. Even with these issues, The Royal Writ succeeds in delivering a distinctive and engaging experience that stands out within the deckbuilding genre. Its combination of strategic positioning, evolving mechanics, and replayable structure creates a gameplay loop that is both challenging and rewarding. For players who enjoy experimenting with systems and refining their strategies over multiple runs, it offers a compelling and memorable experience. Rating: 8/10

I have only played a few hours, but so far there's a huge amount of replayability to see here with two 'acts' providing quite distinct experiences (some different mechanics, different card pools, etc), challenges providing twists on those experiences, and ramping difficulty modifiers to climb through for each act. A few minor downsides: There are a few bugs I've noticed, but nothing game breaking, mostly either purely visual or related to achievements (I got a few that I definitely hadn't achieved). The "stick" that taps your score to reveal it after calculating is just annoying, there's an option to speed it up but why on earth is this even in the game? Finally, when your hand size gets large (lots of consumables can cause this in particular) it can be very difficult to select cards at certain positions in your hand, especially if you want to use a consumable on them. All these are quite minor though, really, and haven't hampered my play experience aside the odd brief frustration.

I really loved this game, and I wanted to share my thoughts and feedback with both potential players and the developers. First of all, I didn't have any high expectations of the game, but the art style caught my attention and it is truly good [h1] Story [/h1] The story follows the Crow King, an anthropomorphic bird(?) ruling a kingdom and expanding his lands further and further. That's actually the whole story. It's quite simple, but it's still interesting to follow, and the game actively keeps you engaged. [h1] Gameplay [/h1] A few words about the mechanics: I'm not fond of deck-builder genres, so I was quite skeptical before I ran it. Here's how the gameplay works: you start with a deck on a battlefield. The field consists of columns and the final column is the base that you need to destroy. Every turn your cards (that you put at the first column) advance further and each new column buffs your card. However, if you hit the final column (the enemy's base), your card will die. The gameplay is based on collecting cards on your way to the boss, defeating them and continuing the cycle. There are tons of things that may happen to your cards and you can create unique combinations. For instance, I had a card that gives me money and boosts morale for each poisoned card, so I made half my deck poisoned and that way I could farm money. [h1] Replayability [/h1] The thing that I found cool is that the game is divided into two Acts and the mechanics in each Act are distinct, which allows you to replay both of them and it feels genuinely different. The story is not that long, but endless mode solves this problem. [h1] Drawbacks [/h1] After all of the above, there are some drawbacks that developers may take into account for their future projects (and I hope there will be more games from them). Maybe it's my personal problem, but it was hard to understand the descriptions of some cards. English is not my native language, so sometimes I switched to Russian to make sure I got everything right, but it didn't clarify much, and the only thing left was to test it in practice. Moreover, there are some cards whose purpose I can't understand even now. Why would I even use them? Some cards can cause freezing or bleeding and I don't know how I'm supposed to use them to gain an advantage. Yes. there is tutorial and manual in game but it lacks details Another small element that I found annoying is that the history of your dead cards shows only their name and the cause of death. But sorry guys, I don't remember what the cards are called. It would be much better if I could hover over the name to see what the card is, or if I could name a card myself, because two the same card types can exist in your deck with the same name. [h1] Final Thoughts [/h1] Honestly, all these drawbacks didn't affect me much and the game still feels amazing and draws me back to try new combinations or find the rest of the unopened cards. I love the art style of the game and it's what initially attracted me to it. Gameplay wise it's fun deck building roguelike turned based map movement. The game is currently split up into multiple "Acts". Acts each have their own arc of the story but, they also have their own mechanics. At the base they are still both deckbuilding roguelikes. Act 1 is fun and and relatively easy to learn. You can play the demo and experience Act 1 to certain extent. Act 2 introduces the morale mechanic. If your morale gets too low it'll cap your board multipliers to 1. Act 2 also has it's own set of cards. So it become a very steep learning curve. I'm still struggling with this mode and for those who want a challenge in deck building this is for you. The game has it's challenge modes which set restrictions as well. The challenges are fun and they aren't ridiculously difficult but, they do force you to think and build than you might normally would. I'd highly recommend you play the demo. If you enjoy it you'll enjoy playing Act 1. They did make balance changes for the cards since the demo. So you'll have to adjust the strategies but, they are mostly the same. Act 2 is why I find it hard to recommend. It's such a steep learning curve that it's not fun. If you enjoyed the demo but still on the fence then wait for a sale. It's definitely worth the money.
